title: Siegard project standard
description: A project's own rules about how its source is arranged, authored by the project and never by this framework. Siegard ships this contract, the pass that holds code to a registry, and the checks that keep a finding answerable to one rule — it ships no rule. A stack's conventions are not a domain's, and a framework that shipped them would prescribe TypeScript to a Go project; the predecessor this comes from did exactly that and its own weakness list said so. It is a registry rather than prose because every finding a review records must cite exactly one rule by its id, and prose cannot be cited: a finding citing no rule is taste with a location attached. Two exclusions are the whole of its scope. First, **no rule here states what the system answers or who may see what** — a status, an error code, a refusal, an authorization outcome. Those are what the business decided, they live in the knowledge base as nodes, and a rule here stating one would put the standard pass and the base-conformance pass in contradiction over the same line: one requiring in code what the other reports as a fact the base does not hold. Second, **no rule carries a severity and nothing here derives a verdict** — the registry's ancestor graded every finding and fed the grade to an approval gate, which made the reviewer the gate. A finding states what it costs; a person decides what that means.

standard.description: This standard's name, as the review that read it records it. One project may hold several — a backend's rules are not a frontend's — and each is named where it is used.

summary.description: One sentence saying what this standard governs, not that it is a standard.

rules.description: Every rule this standard declares, each with an identifier a finding can cite. Ids are unique across the registry: two rules under one id cannot be told apart by the finding that cites it.

elsewhere.description: What this standard deliberately does not hold, and where each of those lives instead. It is written for the reader who looks for a rule, does not find it, and would otherwise conclude nobody thought of it — the same reason a plan declares its uncovered remainder and a review declares the passes that did not run. Nothing validates the destinations, and nothing has to: this is the registry saying out loud which of the three homes a question belongs to.

slug.description: A name reduced to kebab-case. A name that will not reduce is a refusal, not a transliteration.

allOf.$comment: The reverse — a rule decided by reading naming a tool — is refused by bin/deliver.py, which can say so in a sentence a reader acts on.

id.description: How a finding cites this rule. Short and stable: an id that changes orphans every finding that cited it, and a review from last month is read beside the registry as it stands.

statement.description: What the rule requires, as one condition a reader can hold a file to. "Keep the code clean" is not a statement; "a service or controller never constructs a dependency" is.

because.description: What goes wrong when the rule is departed from, as a consequence rather than as the rule restated. It is required because a rule with no stated reason is an arbitrary constraint that nobody can weigh a departure against, and because it is the material a finding's `cost` is written from: the reviewer says what this departure costs here, in the terms this field gives.

decided_by.description: Which half of the standard this rule sits in, and this is the field that decides who applies it. `reading` means telling whether the rule holds requires understanding what the code means — a responsibility that spans two layers, an interface a caller cannot satisfy. Those are the standard pass's, and a review's findings cite them. `tool` means a linter, a compiler, a formatter or a secret scanner decides it exactly and cheaply — a forbidden construct, a name's shape, a file's length, an interpolated query. Those are not a model's work: they run as steps of the caller's own suite, their failures arrive as a captured run, and the failures pass reads what the tool printed. A model applying a rule a linter owns has strictly worse recall than the linter and costs more, and the validator refuses a standard-pass finding that cites one.

tool.description: Which step decides this rule, named as the caller names it to the runner. Required when `decided_by` is `tool`: a rule declared mechanical with nothing named to decide it is a rule nobody applies, which is worse than one nobody wrote.

applies_to.description: Where this rule reaches. A rule with no scope is a rule that fires on every file including the tests, and the finding it produces is one nobody can act on. The scope is stated in parts rather than as a glob pattern so that a validator can check a finding against it without a pattern language: what a glob means differs between tools, and the difference would decide whether a finding is refused.

seen_at.description: A path in this project where the rule is already obeyed. Optional and worth writing: a rule with an example is a rule an implementer can follow without guessing the shape, and it is the same discipline an inventory node applies to a convention — one observed at nowhere is an opinion.

under.description: The directory this scope starts at, relative to the target source root and without a trailing separator.

suffix.description: What a path must end with — an extension, or a role and an extension together such as `.service.ts`.

nested.description: Whether the scope reaches directories below `under`. Absent is false: the scope is exactly the files sitting directly in `under`. This is the distinction a glob language gets wrong in both directions — one tool's single star crosses a separator and another's double star means exactly one directory — so it is stated rather than pattern-matched.

lives_in.description: Where this actually lives — the knowledge base, a named agent of the framework, a tool, or nowhere on purpose.

examples.summary: How this service layers its modules and wires them together.

rules.statement: A constructor receives interfaces, never concrete implementations.
rules.because: A class bound to a concrete collaborator cannot be exercised without it, so a test has to stand up the collaborator's world to assert one line of this one.

rules.statement: Production code logs through the configured logger; console output is not used.
rules.because: A console line goes nowhere in production — no level, no correlation, no retention.

elsewhere.what: Which status a refusal answers with.
elsewhere.lives_in: The knowledge base, as a rule or interface node.
elsewhere.why: It is what the business decided, and stating it here would make two review passes disagree over one line.
